title: roammate vs Facebook Travel Groups: App vs Community
description: Facebook travel groups are the default way to find travel companions, but a purpose-built app like roammate solves problems Facebook can't. Here's the honest comparison.
intro: Facebook travel groups like 'Girls LOVE Travel,' 'Backpacking Southeast Asia,' and dozens of destination-specific groups have been the default way to find travel companions for years. They work — sort of. You post your dates and destination, hope compatible people respond, and figure out the rest through DMs. roammate was built specifically because that process is inefficient, privacy-invasive, and unreliable. But Facebook groups have genuine strengths too. This comparison is honest about both.

sections.heading: Where Facebook Groups Fall Short
sections.content: Facebook groups work on a broadcast model: you post your trip details to hundreds or thousands of strangers and wait for responses. The problem is threefold. First, there's no compatibility filtering. Anyone can respond to your post. Second, privacy is a real issue — to connect with someone on Facebook, you're sharing your full social profile with a stranger. Third, Facebook's algorithm doesn't optimize for your travel needs. Your post competes with memes, ads, and other content for visibility. roammate solves all three problems by design. Profiles are travel-specific, matching is algorithmic, and the entire UX is built around finding a compatible travel companion.

sections.heading: Where Facebook Groups Still Win — and Where roammate Is Better
sections.content: Facebook groups have two genuine advantages. First, volume: groups like 'Backpacking Europe' have hundreds of thousands of members. Second, social proof: you can check a potential companion's Facebook profile and mutual friends. roammate counters both: its matching algorithm means you don't need massive volume to find compatible matches, and profile verification provides identity confirmation without requiring social media exposure. The privacy difference is significant — on Facebook, declining someone's travel invitation means they still have access to your profile. On roammate, they see only your travel profile.
